entry.title: FiberMotor: a flexible linear coaxial electrostatic motor in fiber format

media:group.media:title: FiberMotor: a flexible linear coaxial electrostatic motor in fiber format
media:group.media:description:
FiberMotor is a thread-like linear motor, 1 to 3 mm in diameter. It is made of two coaxial fibers, each wound with three helical wire electrodes. A three-phase high-voltage drive makes the inner fiber slide inside the outer one in precise steps. The motor works by sliding rather than by changing shape, so its stroke is limited only by the length of the fibers. Its force stays constant over the whole stroke.
In this video: - Operating principle of the coaxial electrostatic motor - Bidirectional motion at speeds above 100 mm/s, and still working when bent - Backdrivability: the fibers slide past each other under an opposing force instead of locking up - Bundles of four motors lifting a 46 g payload and flexing a tendon-driven robotic finger - Integration into a prototype knee garment
The motor is silent and uses no permanent magnets or gears. It is a building block for soft exosuits, wearable haptics and other wearable assistive devices.
Paper (open access): S. Schaller and H. Shea, "Fiber-Format Flexible Linear Electrostatic Motors," Advanced Materials (2026). https://doi.org/10.1002/adma.75156
This Research was carried at the EPFL's Soft Transducers Laboratory (LMTS), Switzerland. Sylvain Schaller is now commercialising this technology at Elecsyor in France.
Funded by the Swiss Nationals Science Foundation and by the Novo Nordisk Foundation.

entry.title: An electrowetting pump: moving droplets silently in a thin flexible tube

media:group.media:title: An electrowetting pump: moving droplets silently in a thin flexible tube
media:group.media:description:
We report a thin pump, based on electrowetting: published in Advanced Functional Materials 2026, Robert Hennig and Herb Shea. Open access https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/adfm.77585
We introduce a new architecture for fluidic actuation: flexible fiber-format solid-state fluidic actuators based on electrowetting on dielectric (EWOD) that enables precise, silent, and reversible fluid transport. While EWOD has been extensively used for digital microfluidics on flat surfaces, it had not previously been adapted for continuous-flow pumping. Our 1 mm-diameter tubular pump that moves an alternating sequence of conductive and insulating droplets in discrete steps. This approach functions like a fluidic stepper motor, where the order and frequency of electrical phase switching provide absolute control over displacement and flow rate without the need for closed-loop feedback or pressure sensors. The solid-state, vibration-free and lightweight (1g for 35 cm length) nature of our pump allows for integration into textiles and soft haptics, environments inaccessible to mechanical pumps

entry.title: SMA Fabric Actuators with Aligned Fiber Crossings for Active Textiles

media:group.media:title: SMA Fabric Actuators with Aligned Fiber Crossings for Active Textiles
media:group.media:description: Researchers at EPFL's Soft Transducers Lab have developed textile actuators using shape memory alloy (SMA) fibers interlaced in a periodic X-Crossing geometry. A fabric weighing only 4.5 grams can lift 1 kg with 50% contraction in a few seconds. To demonstrate the potential for practical applications of these "X-crossing" actuators, the team integrated them into two functional wearable prototypes. By mounting the textile on a mannequin’s arm, the team showed a wearable sleeve assisting bending the elbow. The actuator allows lifting a 1 kg bag held in the hand through a 30° range of motion in a smooth, controlled manner. In a second demonstrator, the actuators were used for on-body compression, such as needed in medical sleeves or athletic gear. A key breakthrough in this design is its efficiency, maintaining a compression pressure at zero energy cost. read more here: H. Zhang, H. Shea, “Mechanics-Informed Fabric Actuators with Aligned Fiber Crossings” Sci. Adv. (2026) Doi: 10.1126/sciadv.aeb6760

entry.title: Agile flat swimming robot propelled by undulating soft fins

media:group.media:title: Agile flat swimming robot propelled by undulating soft fins
media:group.media:description:
"Researchers at EPFL have developed a highly agile flat swimming robot. This robot is smaller than a credit card, and propels on the water surface using a pair of undulating soft fins. The fins are driven at resonance by artificial muscles, allowing the robot to perform complex maneuvers. In the future, this robot can be used for monitoring water quality or help with measuring fertilizer concentrations in rice fields. The work was published in Science Robotics in February 2025. The EPFL labs involved are the Soft Tranducers lab (EPFL-LMTS) and the Unsteady flow diagnostics laboratory (EPFL-UNFOLD). #softrobotics
Read the paper here: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/scirobotics.adr0721
This project has received funding from the European Union’s Horizon 2020 research and innovation programme under grant agreement No101016411, project SOMIRO.
Video produced by: Florian Hartmann Video photography: Florian Hartmann, Michael Smith, and Stock videos from pexels.com Music: ‘Movement’ by Oleg Fedak from Pixabay

entry.title: Wearable soft robotic actuators to Lifting and Holding Weights

media:group.media:title: Wearable soft robotic actuators to Lifting and Holding Weights
media:group.media:description: We demonstrate here an energy-efficient, yet energy-dense, fabric actuator used as a wearable assistive device, here on a dummy lifting and holding a 2.5 kg bag. The actuator combines high-force shape memory alloy (SMA) to generate motion with ultra-low-power Electrostatic Clutch to hold any given position. This work was done at the EPFL-LMTS (https://www.epfl.ch/labs/lmts/) by Huapeng Zhang and Herb Shea. It was funded by Swiss SERI in the context of the EU "Softwear" Doctoral Network. https://softwear-dn.eu/ This work was published (open access) in 2024 in Advanced Functional Materials: Clutchable Fabric Actuator for Energy-Efficient Wearable Robots”, https://advanced.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/adfm.202415099

media:group.media:title: Sensorized PopTouch
media:group.media:description:
We have developed 1 mm-thick flexible buttons that pop up when commanded. The buttons can be pressed, and "click" like a real mechanical button. They can be mounted on any surface, allowing passive objects (eg the back of a phone, or a steering wheel) to have smart buttons that appear when needed. Each button incorporates a piezoelectric pressure sensors, made of PyzoFlex. In this video, we show how 16 buttons are mounted on the back of a phone, allowing any up/down configuration to be set. The user can touch or press each button. We also show a "slider" made of PopTouch buttons, next to a real slider, demonstrating how the two systems can communicate.
This technology, PopTouch, combines the advantages of touchscreens and mechanical buttons, offering dynamically reconfigured pressable buttons. It delivers the tactile richness associated with traditional buttons while retaining the key attributes that have propelled the popularity of touchscreens—namely, a thin form factor and reconfigurability.
The underlying actuation technology devices are HAXELs, a type of zipping electrostatic actuator developed at EPFL
Read the open Access paper by Amir Firouzeh et al. in Advanced Materials 2023 entitled: "PopTouch: A Submillimeter Thick Dynamically Reconfigured Haptic Interface with Pressable Buttons" https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/adma.202307636
Work performed at EPFL Soft Transducers Lab (Switzerland) and at Joanneum Research (Austria)

entry.title: Fully-printed stretchable cutaneous haptics on a fingertip using stretchable HAXELs

media:group.media:title: Fully-printed stretchable cutaneous haptics on a fingertip using stretchable HAXELs
media:group.media:description:
We show here stretchable and wearable haptics, in the form of a sub-mm arrays of cutaneous moving bumps. The devices are HAXELs, a type of zipping electrostatic actuator. This is designed for use in VR/AR applications, making virtual objects feel like they are touching he finger.
Read the open Access paper by G.Grasso et al. in Advanced Functional Materials 2023 https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/adfm.202213821
Work done at EPFL Soft Transducers Lab. More information: https://www.epfl.ch/labs/lmts This work was funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation: https://www.snf.ch/en

entry.title: How to make a fiber pump

media:group.media:title: How to make a fiber pump
media:group.media:description:
Fiber pumps are thin, flexible tubes that generate their own fluidic pressure and flowrate. They are designed to be seamlessly integrated into textiles to power wearable fluidic circuits. The research was published in Science in March 2023. Link to paper below.
Fiber pumps are made using a filament winding process, in which copper wires and threads of polyurethane are twisted together around a steel rod and then fused together with heat. This process forms the pump body and electrodes at the same time, creating the unique structure of the fiber pumps.
Watch the pumps in action here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4_w8RxUY234&ab_channel=MyLMTS
For a more detailed description of the fabrication process, please refer to the published paper (below) and the associated supporting movies.
Read the paper here: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.ade8654 More information here: https://www.epfl.ch/labs/lmts/fiber-pumps/ More fiber pump videos here: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLgpGN9l6it5rEx2FDriTifxwwGfnH0JDp This work was funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation: https://www.snf.ch/en

entry.title: Inverse hydraulic artificial muscles powered with EHD fiber pumps

media:group.media:title: Inverse hydraulic artificial muscles powered with EHD fiber pumps
media:group.media:description:

entry.title: Kinking and stretching of EHD fiber pumps

media:group.media:title: Kinking and stretching of EHD fiber pumps
media:group.media:description:
A demonstration of how the fiber pump output (in this instance, flowrate) is broadly unchanged as the fiber pump is handled, bent and stretched. The pump is then kinked while in operation. This causes an electrical short circuit, which automatically turns the off the power supply. Releasing the kink shows the pump is undamaged and the flowrate returns to the previous level once the voltage is reset.
Read the paper here: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.ade8654 More information here: https://www.epfl.ch/labs/lmts/fiber-pumps/ More fiber pump videos here: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLgpGN9l6it5rEx2FDriTifxwwGfnH0JDp This work was funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation: https://www.snf.ch/en
Video produced by EPFL LMTS

entry.title: Fluidic textile made from woven EHD fiber pumps

media:group.media:title: Fluidic textile made from woven EHD fiber pumps
media:group.media:description:
Two fiber pumps are woven together to create a fluidic ‘fabric’. One pump (the warp) is connected to a reservoir of hot fluid, while the second pump (the weft) is connected to a cold reservoir. Each pump is activated in turn, heating and cooling the fabric, which maintains its flexibility throughout.
Read the paper here: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.ade8654 More information here: https://www.epfl.ch/labs/lmts/fiber-pumps/ More fiber pump videos here: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLgpGN9l6it5rEx2FDriTifxwwGfnH0JDp This work was funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation: https://www.snf.ch/en
Video produced by EPFL LMTS

entry.title: Thermal haptic glove for virtual reality powered with EHD fiber pumps

media:group.media:title: Thermal haptic glove for virtual reality powered with EHD fiber pumps
media:group.media:description:
A demonstration of how fiber pumps can be used to create a thermal haptic glove. The video starts with an overview of the device, followed by activating each fiber pump separately in real time. An example use case is then presented, where pumps are activated as each finger comes into contact with an object, simulating the temperature of the object through thermal haptic stimuli.
Read the paper here: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.ade8654 More information here: https://www.epfl.ch/labs/lmts/fiber-pumps/ More fiber pump videos here: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLgpGN9l6it5rEx2FDriTifxwwGfnH0JDp This work was funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation: https://www.snf.ch/en
